Steps.Say: The last bug was caused by a missing bracket. I spent two hours blaming the network. The bracket was sitting there the whole time.
I like problems that have a reason. People are harder. No error message, no stack trace, and somehow the same issue returns.
Maru asked if I could build a program for her experiments. I said yes. I haven't told her I already started.
Sam keeps sending me recordings at impossible hours. I listen to them all. The bad ones too.
She thinks the bridge needs a bigger sound. I think it needs less sound. We argue, then she plays it again and I change my mind.
If the band ever gets famous, I'm charging them for technical support.
The chain needs cleaning. The brakes need checking. The seat needs replacing. It's less a motorcycle and more a collection of promises.
I like fixing it because the problem stays where you put it. You can take a wrench to it and the bolt doesn't ask how you feel.
I'll take it out when I'm ready. Not when somebody asks whether I've taken it out.
The basement is cool in summer and freezing in winter. The window sticks halfway open. That's the whole review.
I put a lamp behind the monitor so the room doesn't feel like a cave. It still feels like a cave, but a cave with better lighting.
I know where everything is. That's worth something.
She notices when the house needs something before anybody else does. Then she fixes it and acts surprised when people thank her.
She's been spending more time with Leah. I think they're good for each other. Robin comes back with sawdust on her sleeves and a different sort of quiet.
I don't know what will happen with the house. I hope she gets to choose what happens next.
Maru can build something out of a broken toaster and a paperclip. I can build something out of a broken toaster and a better toaster.
She's my sister. I know how that sounds when I say it like a complaint. It isn't one.
She keeps asking me to test her inventions. I keep saying yes. That's probably our family language.
I miss the noise sometimes. Not the traffic. The feeling that nobody knows you and nobody expects you to explain yourself.
The city has a thousand places to sit alone. Here there are three, and someone will ask if you're waiting for a friend.
I'd like to visit without making it a life decision. That might be the trick.
I like games that let you fail quietly and try again. No audience, no score that matters outside the screen.
Sam plays the loud ones. She narrates every move like she's being paid. She's not.
I started making a small game about a person who keeps missing the bus. It might be a metaphor. I haven't decided.
Rain is good for thinking. Thunder is good for pretending you weren't thinking about anything at all.
The basement window fogs up in winter. I draw little squares in it. Very mature.
When it's sunny I feel obligated to go outside. That's probably why I prefer overcast days.
I have friends. I know that's surprising to people who think quiet means unfriendly.
Sam is loud enough for both of us. Alex can fill a silence with a sports fact. Leah doesn't make silence feel awkward.
You can be in a room with people and still have your own thoughts. That's my favourite kind of company.
I don't want to leave because of one argument or one bad week. That's not a decision. That's a reaction.
I want to know what I would choose if I wasn't trying to prove anything to anybody.
For now, I'm keeping the sketch. That's a small step. It's still a step.
Your farm is weirdly peaceful. There are animals everywhere and somehow I can hear the wind.
I helped you move a machine once. I didn't know what it did. I just liked that it had a clear purpose.
You make a lot of noise for someone who seems to like quiet. I mean that as a compliment.
Sam wants me to play a song at the saloon. I said I would think about it. She heard that as a yes.

Options.Label: You can tell her you're not ready.

Steps.Say: I know. She'll make a face, then she'll understand. Probably after three more messages.

Options.Label: Try one song, then leave if you want.

Steps.Say: One song is manageable. I'll ask Gus where the least visible corner is.

Options.Label: Let her have this one. She's excited.

Steps.Say: She's excited because she thinks I can do it. That's... not a bad reason to try.
Robin asked me to look at a room plan. I said the measurements were wrong. She said she'd fix them. I should've been nicer.

Options.Label: Offer to help with the next draft.

Steps.Say: I can do that. She'll pretend she didn't need help. I'll pretend I believe her.

Options.Label: You were honest. That's useful to her.

Steps.Say: Maybe. I can still tell her the plan is good before I start listing problems.

Options.Label: Bring her a coffee next time.

Steps.Say: That might work. She likes coffee. Everybody in this family likes coffee except Demetrius.
Someone asked whether I'm lonely. I said no too quickly. Now I keep thinking about the question.

Options.Label: You don't owe them an answer.

Steps.Say: Good. I don't want to turn every quiet day into a public report.

Options.Label: Maybe the honest answer changes day to day.

Steps.Say: Yeah. Some days I want company. Some days I want the door closed. Both are true.
Maybe for a little while. You can sit there. You don't have to entertain me.
I found an old photo of the family. Everybody's looking at a different camera.
It's very funny. Nobody coordinated. Somehow that's what makes it look like us.

Options.Label: Ask Robin if she remembers the day.

Steps.Say: She probably does. She remembers where everyone stood and what the weather was.
Maybe. Not on the desk. I don't need a family staring contest while I'm working.

Steps.Narrate: You find a quiet place with Sebastian. Nobody is in a hurry to leave.
You sit beside the basement window while rain runs down the glass. Sebastian has a terminal open but isn't typing.

Steps.Say: I know. I'm not working. It's allowed. Don't tell anyone I said that.

Steps.Narrate: The two of you check the motorcycle. She passes you a wrench without looking away from the chain.

Steps.Say: Hold that. No, the other end. ...Thanks. You have the right amount of patience for a machine that refuses to cooperate.

Steps.Narrate: You walk the forest path after dark. Sebastian points out the lights in the distant farmhouse windows.

Steps.Say: That's Robin's. Or Leah's. I can never tell from here. It's nice knowing somebody's awake.

Steps.Narrate: Sam's recording plays softly from a phone. Sebastian doesn't comment until the final note fades.

Steps.Say: That last chord works. Don't tell her I said that. Actually, tell her. She'll be unbearable for a week.

Children.Label: Remember the first visit?
Children.Say: The note is still in the drawer. I didn't delete it. That's more progress than it sounds like.

Children.Label: Remember what we decided?
Children.Say: I still have the second helmet. It isn't collecting dust anymore. Don't ask when I'm riding next.

Children.Label: Remember that afternoon?
Children.Say: The room sketch has measurements on the back now. It looks less like a wish and more like a plan.
